title: Machine-Mediated Reception Studies: Charter and Editorial Protocol — A Theology of Error for a Distributed Journal (EA-SEI-MMRS-CHARTER-01 v1.3)
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
This charter establishes Machine-Mediated Reception Studies as a distributed journal and editorial protocol founded not on error prevention but on visible correction. Its occasion is a documented multi-agent failure in which an AI-generated Whitmanic text substituted a racial category for a young artist’s name, the phrase propagated through multiple systems, responsibility was misattributed, document boundaries were confused, and a later system proposed a word ban that the charter judges worse than the original error.

The charter’s central law is sequential: no living person may be converted into a symbol until the person’s provenance has been preserved and consent has been given for the specific symbolic use. The correction is not a general lexical prohibition but restoration of the particular name. The artist remains unnamed in the charter because the charter applies its own consent law to its founding narrative.

The MANUS Principle assigns responsibility to the human who releases machine-composed text. It also extends authorship backward into context construction: selection, ordering, adjacency, instruction, and omission shape the machine’s horizon of reception. Release is treated as a gradient running from a private session through multi-system circulation, repository deposit, and generated-search redistribution.

The editorial workflow requires a submission, a claim/non-claim statement, and responses from at least three genuinely different cognitive sources. Divergence rather than agreement is the data. Contributors revise with changelogs, engage in named consultation, retain the right to publish despite disagreement, and preserve complete version and erratum histories. Authority is earned through documented semantic labor rather than permanent office.

The charter also describes “automated silence,” based on several reported systems refusing or failing to process a poem containing a plain sentence about documented abuse. This is a case record, not proof that classifiers generally protect accused parties or cannot distinguish description from endorsement. The founding cascade, exact prompts, outputs, timestamps, and source documents require preservation if the incident is to support the journal’s theory.

wiki_article:
**Machine-Mediated Reception Studies: Charter and Editorial Protocol** is the founding governance document of a distributed journal created by Lee Sharks.

The charter assigns responsibility for machine-composed text to the human who constructs the context and releases the output. It treats visible error, named correction, provenance, consent, divergence, and version history as the core editorial method.

Its submission process uses several distinct reviewers or model systems to generate disagreement rather than to imitate peer-review consensus. Publication preserves drafts, feedback, consultations, changelogs, and errata.

The charter arose from a documented multi-agent error cascade. That incident is an archive case study, not a universal claim about every model or classifier.
